title: Revisiting Anisotropy in Language Transformers: The Geometry of Learning Dynamics
claim: Embedding spread shrinks with token frequency across model families, and this effect appears during training and is weaker in some architectures.
layout: 1 trajectory panel plus 2x5 grid of hexbin scatters, left-to-right
description: A wide figure with a tall line plot on the left and a 2x5 grid of hexbin scatter plots to its right. The left panel, titled pythia-410m, plots distance to centroid against training step. Solid blue lines show the most frequent tokens and dashed red lines show the least frequent tokens. The red lines start high and drop, and the blue lines drop lower and plateau. Each scatter panel shows one model: Pythia 160m, 410m, 1b and 1.4b, SmolLM2 360M and 1.7B, and EuroBERT 210m and 610m. The x-axis is log frequency and the y-axis is mean or relative distance to centroid. Purple hexbins have a red LOWESS fit line that slopes downward for the decoders. A box in each panel lists the Spearman and Pearson correlations. The EuroBERT-610m panels are flatter and also show max and min distance. The eye goes first to the red fit lines and the steep trajectories.
caption: Temporal dynamics of embedding variance across model architectures. Left: Training trajectories for the top-5 most frequent versus bottom-5 least frequent tokens in Pythia-410m, illustrating the tighter confinement of frequent tokens. Middle: Mean Euclidean distance to centroid vs. log-frequency for Pythia (160m, 410m, 1b, 1.4b), SmoLLM2 (360m, 1.7b), and EuroBERT (210m, 610m). Causal decoders exhibit a strong negative correlation (Pearson $\rho \approx -0.5$), confirming frequency-induced variance collapse. Rightmost: Detailed Min/Max distance statistics for EuroBERT-610m. Although the mean trend is attenuated, the distributional view still shows a weaker frequency-dependent concentration pattern.
abstract: Since their introduction, Transformer architectures have dominated Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, recent research has highlighted an inherent anisotropy phenomenon in these models, presenting a significant challenge to their geometric interpretation. Previous theoretical studies on this phenomenon are rarely grounded in the underlying representation geometry. In this paper, we extend them by deriving geometric arguments for how frequency-biased sampling attenuates curvature visibility and why training preferentially amplify tangent directions. Empirically, we then use concept-based mechanistic interpretability during training, rather than only post hoc, to fit activation-derived low-rank tangent proxies and test them against ordinary backpropagated true gradients. Across encoder-style and decoder-style language models, we find that these activation-derived directions capture both unusually large gradient energy and a substantially larger share of gradient anisotropy than matched-rank normal controls, providing strong empirical support for a tangent-aligned account of anisotropy.
